summary: Bernal Heights is a hill of short steep streets, and most of the record is the work of making them: grades set and re-set on Aztec, Coso, Rutledge and Franconia, sewers dug under them, and in 1921 the first concrete pavement laid anywhere in San Francisco — a plain six-inch slab on Winfield Street. It did not always hold. Mrs. Volhart of 28 Aztec Street came down to object to a change of grade in 1939; in 1960 the owner of 37 Elsie Street told the Board the work had injured his property by sliding the embankment in the rain. Where the slope beat the roadway the city built stairs instead — up Tompkins Avenue in 1964, on the way to a school, and up Peralta Avenue in 1973 with the gas company sharing the cost. Before 1930 the hill still kept animals, fifty horses behind 3142 Mission Street and a cow at the back of 230 Prospect Avenue, and from 1916 the Board began refusing stables outright. It lit the hill a lamp at a time — one arc lamp at Ellsworth and Cortland in 1909, the whole spine of Cortland Avenue corner by named corner in 1927. The top of the hill took longer: the boulevard round the summit was ordered in 1929 and the land under it then bought a lot at a time through the 1930s, $100 and $200 a parcel, while on the south side a cut was driven through and the houses in its way sold off. Le Conte School went up on Harrison Street in 1924, and two years later its teacher in charge was given permission to rope off Norwich Street at recess. From the 1980s the city bought the slopes back for open space and began naming the trees on them — the blue elderberry at Folsom Street, the two flowering ashes outside the Bernal Heights Library, which had started life in a rented building on Cortland Avenue in 1936. Through the same years most of the new paperwork has been Mission Street and the lanes off it being split into condominiums, one final map at a time. In 2026 the Board voted a plaque into the sidewalk at 205 Mullen Avenue, where Carlos Santana was living when he was first discovered.
